title: Do not kill
hookLine: Jesus deepens it to anger and contempt (Matthew 5:22)

lines: THE WORD YOU CALL YOUR BROTHER.
cards: "Thou shalt not kill." On paper it can sound like the easiest commandment on the list. Get through the day without killing anyone, and you're finished.
Then Jesus sees the crowds, goes up a mountain and sits down, his disciples come to him, and he moves the line. Not just the knife. The anger.
Not just the act. The word you call your brother.

teach.h: THEM OF OLD TIME, AND JESUS.
teach.b: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says: "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill." Then he goes further.

"But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment." He goes on to an insult, Raca, which the King James leaves untranslated, and then to "Thou fool."
He isn't saying anger and murder are the same thing. He's tracing murder back to its root. Before a hand ever moves, a heart decides that someone doesn't count.
Contempt is the seed: a fool, a nobody, a waste of space. That's the word that makes harm thinkable. Then he turns practical.

If you're about to worship and remember that someone has something against you: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."
Some translations render the commandment you shall not murder, reading it as unlawful killing. Christians disagree, seriously and in good faith, about war, self-defense and the death penalty.
Mennonite and Quaker traditions teach nonviolence. Other churches teach that force can sometimes be just.
Jesus's reading puts all of them in front of the same test, closer to home than any battlefield: the contempt we let ourselves say.

how: Christians read this commandment alongside the Sermon on the Mount, so preaching on it often turns to anger, insult and reconciliation; churches differ on war and the death penalty, with Mennonites and Quakers holding to nonviolence and others teaching just-war principles.

games.why: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother." repair comes before ritual.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off, a coworker, a relative, a driver from this morning, and notice the word you use for them in your head.

Hold that word up, then try calling them what Jesus does, a brother, a sister; you don't have to like them, just set the word down. If you pray, you can pray for them, using their name instead of the word.

wordCard.voice: Do not kill. The commandment against taking life, which Jesus traces back to anger and contempt in the heart.

orig.note: Hebrew: you shall not murder, or kill. The words of Exodus 20:13.

carryVoice: Your line: not even in the heart. Contempt is where it starts, so that's where it stops. See you tomorrow.
